title: The Story of the First Old Man and of the Hind
paragraphs: Now I will begin my story (said the old man), so listen carefully.
This hind you see with me is my wife. We had no children of our own, so I adopted the son of a slave I was fond of, and made up my mind to leave him everything.

My wife, though, hated both the mother and the child, and she hid it from me until it was too late. When the boy was about ten, I had to go away on a journey. Before leaving, I put the mother and child in my wife’s care and asked her to look after them while I was gone, which turned out to be a whole year. In that time she studied magic, to carry out her wicked plan. Once she had learned enough, she took my son to a faraway place and turned him into a calf. Then she handed him to my steward and told him to take care of a calf she had bought. She also turned the slave into a cow and sent her to the steward too.
When I came home I asked after my slave and the boy. “Your slave is dead,” my wife said, “and as for your son, I haven’t seen him for two months, and I have no idea where he is.”

I was sad to hear that my slave had died, but since my son had only gone missing, I thought I would soon find him. Eight months went by, though, and there was still no word of him. Then the feast of Bairam arrived.

To mark it, I told my steward to bring me a very fat cow to sacrifice. He did. The cow he brought was my poor slave. I tied her up, but just as I was about to kill her, she began to low most pitifully, and I saw her eyes streaming with tears. It struck me as very strange, and, moved by pity, I told the steward to take her away and bring another. My wife was there, and she mocked my softness, which in the end did her malice no good. “What are you doing?” she cried. “Kill this cow. She’s the best we have for the sacrifice.”
To please her, I tried a second time, but again the animal’s lowing and tears disarmed me.
“Take her away,” I told the steward, “and kill her yourself. I can’t.”
The steward killed her, but when he skinned her he found nothing but bones, though she had looked so fat. I was annoyed.
“Keep her for yourself,” I told the steward, “and if you have a fat calf, bring me that instead.”

Soon he brought me a very fat calf, which, though I did not know it, was my son. It struggled hard to break its rope and get to me. It threw itself at my feet with its head on the ground, as if it wanted to win my pity and beg me not to take its life.
This sight surprised and touched me even more than the cow’s tears had done.
“Go,” I told the steward, “take this calf back and look after it well, and at once bring me a different one in its place.”
As soon as my wife heard me say this, she cried out, “What are you doing, husband? Don’t sacrifice any calf but this one.”
“Wife,” I answered, “I will not sacrifice this calf.” And despite all her protests, I stood firm.
I had another calf killed, and this one was led away. On the following day the steward asked if he could talk to me alone.

“I’ve come,” he said, “to bring you some news that I think you’ll be glad to hear. I have a daughter who knows magic. Yesterday, as I was taking back the calf you refused to sacrifice, I noticed her smile, and then straight away start to cry. I asked her why.”

“Father,” she answered, “this calf is our master’s son. I smile from joy at seeing him still alive, and I cry at the thought of his mother, who was sacrificed yesterday as a cow. It was our master’s wife who did this to them, because she hated the mother and her son.”

“When I heard this, O genie,” the old man went on, “you can imagine how astonished I was. I went at once with the steward to speak to his daughter myself. First I went to the stable to see my son, and he answered all my caresses in his own dumb way. When the steward’s daughter came, I asked her whether she could turn my son back into his true shape.”
“Yes, I can,” she replied, “on two conditions. The first is that you give him to me as my husband, and the second is that you let me punish the woman who turned him into a calf.”
“To the first condition,” I answered, “I agree with all my heart, and I will give you a generous dowry. To the second I agree as well. I only beg you to spare her life.”
“I will,” she replied. “I will treat her as she treated your son.”
Then she took a vessel of water and spoke some words over it that I did not understand. When she threw the water over him, he instantly became a young man again.
“My son, my dear son,” I cried, kissing him in a rush of joy. “This kind girl has freed you from a terrible enchantment, and I am sure that out of gratitude you will marry her.”

He agreed happily. But before the wedding, the girl turned my wife into a hind, and that is who stands before you now. I wanted her to have this shape rather than a stranger one, so that we could still see her about the family without disgust.

Since then my son has lost his wife and gone off traveling. I am now searching for him, and since I did not want to leave my wife in other people’s care, I am taking her with me. Is this not a most marvelous tale?
“It is indeed,” said the genie, “and because of it I grant you a third of this merchant’s punishment.”

When the first old man had finished, the second, who was leading the two black dogs, spoke to the genie. “I will tell you what happened to me, and I am sure you will find my story even more astonishing than the one you have just heard. But when I have told it, will you grant me too a third of the merchant’s punishment?”
“Yes,” replied the genie, “as long as your story is better than the hind’s.”
On those terms, the second old man began.
